title: Transport in Plants
tagline: How water, minerals and food move through a plant: diffusion, osmosis, water potential, the ascent of sap in the xylem, translocation in the phloem, transpiration and the plant's water relationships.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ISC Class XI Biology syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). Syllabus unit and chapter title were taken from the official-verified ISC Biology registry; no board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original BoardPrep practice and not a previous year question. The official CISCE ISC Class XI Biology syllabus includes Transport in Plants as a prescribed chapter, so the content follows that syllabus framing.

overview.intro: A plant is not a set of isolated cells; it is a connected system in which water, minerals and food must move from one part to another. The tallest tree presents an obvious puzzle: how does water reach the leaves, and how does food made in the leaves reach the roots? This chapter answers that question at the level appropriate to ISC Class XI. It begins with the simplest movements, diffusion and osmosis, then builds to water potential, the movement of water through the plant, the transport of food in the phloem, and the loss of water by transpiration. The central idea is that transport depends on both physical principles and plant structure.

facts.label: Core ideas
facts.value: Diffusion; osmosis; water potential; plasmolysis; imbibition; xylem transport; cohesion-tension mechanism; transpiration; stomata; phloem translocation; source-sink relationship

learningOutcomes: Explain diffusion and osmosis as basic means of movement in plants.
Define water potential and explain its role in water movement.
Describe plasmolysis and imbibition and their significance.
Explain how water is transported through the xylem from roots to leaves.
Explain the cohesion-tension idea as the basis of the ascent of sap.
Describe transpiration and the role of stomata.
Explain translocation of food in the phloem and the source-sink idea.
Distinguish between xylem transport and phloem translocation.

blocks.text: The simplest means of movement in plants are diffusion and osmosis. Diffusion is the net movement of molecules from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration. It does not require a membrane, and it is important for gases such as oxygen and carbon dioxide. Osmosis is the special case in which water moves across a semipermeable membrane from a region of higher water potential to a region of lower water potential. Osmosis is central to plant water relations because it helps explain how cells take up water and how water moves between cells.

items: Diffusion is movement down a concentration gradient.
Osmosis is diffusion of water across a semipermeable membrane.
Water moves from higher to lower water potential.
Osmosis is important in plant cell water uptake.
Both processes are passive and do not require direct energy input.

items.text: If a plant cell is placed in pure water, water may enter by osmosis because the cell contents have a lower water potential than the surrounding water. The cell swells and becomes turgid if the wall can resist the pressure.
items.note: The example connects osmosis to the everyday idea of a plant becoming firm or swollen.

learn.title: Water potential and plant water relations

blocks.text: Water potential is a way of describing the tendency of water to move from one place to another. Pure water has the highest water potential, and adding solutes lowers it. Pressure also affects water potential. In plant tissues, water moves from regions of higher water potential to regions of lower water potential, so the concept helps explain movement into roots, across cells, and up the xylem. A useful way to remember water potential is that it combines the effects of solutes and pressure into one guiding idea: water moves toward the lower potential.

items: Water potential indicates the tendency of water to move.
Pure water has the highest water potential.
Solutes lower water potential.
Pressure affects water potential in plant cells.
Water moves toward lower water potential.

items.text: If the soil around roots has a higher water potential than the root cells, water can move into the roots. If the plant loses water faster than it can take it up, the water potential in the tissues changes and wilting may occur.
items.note: The example connects water potential to a visible plant response.

blocks.text: When a plant cell loses water by osmosis in a hypertonic environment, the cytoplasm shrinks away from the cell wall. This is plasmolysis, and it helps explain why plants wilt or why some preserved foods do not support microbial growth as easily. The reverse process, deplasmolysis, can occur if the cell is returned to a less concentrated environment, provided the damage is not permanent. Another related phenomenon is imbibition, the absorption of water by solids such as seeds and wood, which causes them to swell. Imbibition is not osmosis, but it is important in the early uptake of water by seeds.

items: Plasmolysis is the shrinkage of cytoplasm from the cell wall due to water loss.
Deplasmolysis is the reversal when water re-enters.
Imbibition is water absorption by solids, causing swelling.
Imbibition is important in seed germination.
These phenomena are related to, but not identical with, osmosis.

items.text: If a dry seed is placed in water, it swells partly by imbibition before active growth begins. If a plant cell is placed in strong salt solution, it may plasmolyse and become flaccid.
items.note: The example distinguishes imbibition from osmosis and connects both to familiar observations.

learn.title: Ascent of sap in the xylem

blocks.text: Water and dissolved minerals move upward through the xylem from the roots to the stems and leaves. The pulling force comes mainly from transpiration at the leaves. As water evaporates from the leaf surfaces, tension is created in the water column in the xylem. Because water molecules cohere to one another and adhere to the walls of the xylem vessels, the column can be pulled upward without breaking easily. This is the cohesion-tension mechanism. It explains how water can reach great heights without a pump in the ordinary sense.

items: Xylem transports water and minerals upward.
Transpiration produces a pulling force.
Cohesion between water molecules helps maintain a continuous column.
Adhesion to xylem walls also matters.
The ascent of sap is explained mainly by the cohesion-tension mechanism.

items.text: Think of the water column in the xylem like a rope being pulled from above. If the water molecules stuck together well and did not break apart easily, the pull at the top could draw water up from below. That is the basic idea behind the cohesion-tension explanation.
items.note: The analogy makes the cohesion-tension mechanism easier to visualize.

blocks.text: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the plant, mainly through stomata in the leaves. It is often seen as a problem because it wastes water, but it has important functions: it helps pull water upward, it cools the plant, and it helps move minerals. Stomata open and close to regulate gas exchange and water loss. Their opening and closing depends on the state of the guard cells. Transpiration is therefore not just a leak; it is a controlled process with significant consequences for the whole plant.

items: Transpiration is loss of water vapour from the plant.
It occurs mainly through stomata.
It helps pull water up the xylem.
Stomata regulate gas exchange and water loss.
Guard cells control stomatal opening and closing.

items.text: On a hot dry day, a plant may close its stomata to reduce water loss, but this also limits carbon dioxide entry and therefore photosynthesis. The plant thus faces a trade-off between saving water and making food.
items.note: The example shows that transpiration control is a balance, not a simple on-off switch.

blocks.text: Food, mainly in the form of sugars made by photosynthesis, moves through the phloem from a source to a sink. A source is a part of the plant that produces or releases food, such as a photosynthesizing leaf. A sink is a part that uses or stores food, such as a growing root, fruit, or storage organ. Unlike the mainly upward flow in the xylem, phloem translocation can go in different directions depending on where the sources and sinks are. The movement is linked to the loading and unloading of sugars and the resulting pressure differences.

items: Phloem translocates food, especially sugars.
Movement is from source to sink.
Source and sink can change depending on the season and plant needs.
Translocation is not restricted to upward flow.
Pressure differences help drive phloem movement.

items.text: In a growing plant, a mature leaf may act as a source, while a developing fruit acts as a sink. Later, a storage root may become a sink in one season and a source in another. The same tissue is not fixed forever as source or sink.
items.note: The example corrects the idea that source and sink are fixed locations.

learn.title: Comparing xylem and phloem and common mistakes

blocks.text: A common mistake in this chapter is to assume that xylem transports only water and phloem transports only food, and that one always moves upward and the other always downward. In reality, xylem conducts water and minerals upward in the main, while phloem translocates organic nutrients from source to sink, which can be upward or downward. Another frequent error is to treat transpiration as a useless loss only, or to confuse osmosis, diffusion and active transport. The best answer usually starts from the function, then explains the physical principle involved.

items: Xylem mainly conducts water and minerals upward.
Phloem translocates food from source to sink.
Phloem flow can be bidirectional.
Transpiration has both costs and benefits.
Osmosis, diffusion and active transport are not the same.

items.text: If a student says all water movement in plants is by osmosis alone, that is inaccurate. Osmosis is important at the cellular level, but long-distance upward movement also depends on physical forces in the xylem, especially transpiration pull and cohesion.
items.note: The example distinguishes between local and long-distance transport clearly.

keyPoints: Diffusion and osmosis are basic passive means of movement in plants.
Water potential helps explain the direction of water movement.
Plasmolysis and imbibition are related but distinct phenomena.
Water moves upward in the xylem mainly by the cohesion-tension mechanism.
Transpiration creates the pull and is regulated through stomata.
Phloem translocates food from source to sink.
Source and sink can change with season and plant needs.
Xylem and phloem have different substances and different flow patterns.
examFocus: Do not say phloem always moves food downward.
Do not treat transpiration as only a waste process.
Explain osmosis and diffusion separately and correctly.
Link ascent of sap to transpiration pull, cohesion and adhesion.
Use water potential carefully as a guiding concept for water movement.

vocabulary.meaning: Net movement of molecules from higher to lower concentration.
Movement of water across a semipermeable membrane from higher to lower water potential.
A measure of the tendency of water to move from one place to another.
Shrinkage of the cytoplasm from the cell wall due to water loss.
Absorption of water by solids causing them to swell.
The tissue that mainly conducts water and minerals upward.
The tissue that mainly translocates food from source to sink.
Loss of water vapour from a plant, mainly through stomata.
Pores in the leaf surface that regulate gas exchange and water loss.
A part of the plant that produces or releases food for translocation.
A part of the plant that uses or stores translocated food.

questions.prompt: Osmosis is best defined as the movement of water:
options: From higher solute concentration to lower solute concentration
Across a semipermeable membrane from higher to lower water potential
Against a concentration gradient using energy
questions.answer: Across a semipermeable membrane from higher to lower water potential
questions.explanation: Osmosis is the diffusion of water across a semipermeable membrane toward lower water potential.
questions.commonMistake: Defining osmosis only in terms of solute concentration without the membrane and water potential idea.

questions.prompt: The movement of water into a plant root from the soil depends mainly on:
questions.explanation: Water moves according to water potential differences.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking root water uptake depends on leaf shape or soil colour.

questions.prompt: Plasmolysis occurs when a plant cell is placed in a:
questions.explanation: In a hypertonic solution, the cell loses water and the cytoplasm shrinks from the wall.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing hypertonic and hypotonic effects on the cell.

questions.prompt: The main tissue that conducts water and minerals upward in a plant is:
questions.explanation: Xylem conducts water and minerals upward.

options: Pulling water upward through the xylem
questions.answer: Pulling water upward through the xylem
questions.explanation: Transpiration pull is a key force in the upward movement of water.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking transpiration only affects leaves and has no effect on water movement.

questions.prompt: Stomata mainly help the plant to:
options: Regulate gas exchange and water loss
questions.answer: Regulate gas exchange and water loss
questions.explanation: Stomata regulate gas exchange and water loss.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking stomata are only for water loss or only for photosynthesis.

questions.prompt: Which idea best explains the upward movement of water in tall plants?
options: Active pumping by root hairs alone
Osmosis in every cell along the path only
questions.explanation: The cohesion-tension mechanism explains the ascent of sap.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking root pressure or osmosis alone can fully explain upward water movement in tall plants.

questions.prompt: In phloem translocation, a sink is a part of the plant that:
questions.explanation: A sink is a part that uses or stores translocated food.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking a sink is only a root or only a leaf.

questions.prompt: Which statement about source and sink in plants is correct?
options: A leaf is always a source and a root is always a sink
Source and sink can change depending on season and plant needs
questions.answer: Source and sink can change depending on season and plant needs
questions.explanation: Source and sink roles are not fixed permanently.
questions.commonMistake: Treating source and sink as fixed locations.

questions.explanation: Imbibition is the swelling of dry materials like seeds when they absorb water.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing imbibition with osmosis or thinking it is unimportant.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between xylem transport and phloem translocation.
questions.answer: Xylem mainly conducts water and minerals upward, while phloem translocates food from source to sink and can move in different directions.
questions.explanation: The two tissues differ in substance transported and direction of flow.
questions.commonMistake: Saying both tissues transport only water or only food.

questions.prompt: Why is transpiration considered useful despite causing water loss?
questions.answer: Because it helps pull water and minerals upward, cools the plant, and assists in transport.
questions.explanation: Transpiration has useful functions, not just a cost.

questions.answer: It is the idea that water is pulled up the xylem because water molecules cohere to one another and adhere to the walls, while transpiration creates tension at the top.
questions.explanation: Cohesion and adhesion help a water column survive being pulled upward.
questions.commonMistake: Explaining ascent of sap without mentioning cohesion or tension.

questions.prompt: If a plant wilts on a hot day, the most likely immediate cause is:
options: Excessive water uptake pulling cells apart
questions.explanation: Wilting occurs when water loss is faster than replacement.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking wilting is caused mainly by too much water uptake.

options: Water entering a plant cell from pure water
Water moving across a semipermeable membrane
Movement of water down its water potential gradient
questions.explanation: Dry seeds swelling is imbibition, not osmosis.
questions.commonMistake: Treating imbibition as a form of osmosis.
